noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: practical: investigate the effect of light on net gas exchange from a leaf, using hydrogen-carbonate indicator

primer.text: Hydrogen-carbonate indicator is a CO2 gauge you can read by colour. Four boiling tubes, four light treatments and a leaf apiece let you watch a plant's net exchange swing with the light — the daylight-darkness story of the previous notes, bottled and observable.

lessons.title: Why Light Changes Net Exchange
sourceHeadings: Practical: The Effect of Light on Gas Exchange in Plants
lessons.opening: The experiment compares leaves under four light regimes: full light, darkness behind foil, dim light behind muslin, and a control tube with no leaf at all. The indicator's colour law carries the information — yellow means carbon dioxide has accumulated above atmospheric levels, orange means atmospheric, purple means the leaf has drawn carbon dioxide below atmospheric levels.
keyPoints: The tubes compare photosynthesis and respiration under different light treatments.
Hydrogen-carbonate indicator turns yellow at high CO2, orange at atmospheric, purple at low.
Tube A holds no leaf and acts as the control in bright light.
Tube B sits in bright light, tube C is foil-wrapped for darkness, tube D wears muslin for dim light.
Each tube takes a fixed volume of indicator, bunged and left for hours or overnight.

low.restatement: Light decides whether the leaf drains carbon dioxide or fills the tube with it.
low.analogy: Four windows with different curtains: the room's temperature tells you which curtain was open.
low.examPointer: Memorise the colour scale in order — yellow, orange, purple — against rising, normal, falling CO2.

medium.restatement: Each tube isolates one light condition; the control isolates none at all.
medium.analogy: A line-up of suspects with one innocent bystander — the control — for comparison.
medium.examPointer: Name every tube's treatment when describing the setup; partial descriptions lose marks.

check.stem: What colour shows carbon dioxide above atmospheric levels?

options.explanation: Extra CO2 dissolves and acidifies, driving the indicator yellow.
Purple means carbon dioxide has fallen below atmospheric.
Orange is the atmospheric baseline.
Blue plays no part in this indicator's scale.

check.stem: Which tube is the control?

options.explanation: Without a leaf nothing alters the indicator, so it proves the baseline.
Tube B holds a photosynthesising leaf.
Tube C holds a leaf in darkness.
Tube D holds a leaf in dim light.

check.stem: What does the foil wrapped around tube C ensure?

options.text: No light reaches the leaf, so photosynthesis stops
options.explanation: Darkness removes photosynthesis, leaving respiration alone.
Insulation is not the foil's purpose.

options.text: Carbon dioxide cannot enter the tube
options.explanation: The bung seals the tube; the foil only blocks light.
Evaporation is not part of the design.

check.stem: Why does tube D wear muslin rather than foil?

options.text: To let some light through, creating a dim-light treatment
options.explanation: The muslin dims the light instead of removing it.
Moisture is not the muslin's role.
Gases move freely through cloth.
Weight is irrelevant to the design.

check.stem: How much hydrogen-carbonate indicator goes into each tube?

options.explanation: The fixed volume keeps the tubes comparable.
The stated volume is twenty.

options.text: Enough to cover the leaf completely
options.explanation: The volume is fixed, not leaf-dependent.
Variation would break the comparison.

check.stem: State the indicator's colour at high, atmospheric and low carbon dioxide.
check.modelAnswer: Yellow at high, orange at atmospheric, purple at low carbon dioxide.

check.stem: List the four tubes' light treatments.
check.modelAnswer: A: no leaf in bright light; B: leaf in bright light; C: leaf in darkness under foil; D: leaf in dim light under muslin.

check.stem: Explain why a control tube with no leaf is needed.
check.modelAnswer: Because it shows what the indicator does with no leaf present — nothing: it stays orange at atmospheric carbon dioxide; any colour change in the other tubes can then be blamed on the leaf's exchange rather than the indicator drifting on its own.

check.stem: A student wraps tube B in foil by mistake and wraps tube C's foil loosely. Predict the observed colours and the error's effect.
check.modelAnswer: The mis-wrapped B turns yellow like a darkness tube, because its leaf only respires; the loosely foiled C lets some light in, so its indicator may stay orange or turn slightly purple; the error swaps the two treatments, scrambling which conclusion belongs to which condition.

lessons.title: Reading the Results
lessons.opening: After hours or overnight the colours tell the story. The control stays orange. The bright-light leaf turns purple, because photosynthesis outruns respiration and drains carbon dioxide below atmospheric. The dark-wrapped leaf turns yellow, because respiration alone keeps feeding carbon dioxide into the sealed air. The dim-muslin leaf sits near balance: orange, or shading towards purple.
keyPoints: Tube A stays orange: no leaf, no change.
Tube B turns purple: photosynthesis exceeds respiration, so carbon dioxide falls below atmospheric.
Tube C turns yellow: respiration alone, so carbon dioxide climbs above atmospheric.
Tube D stays orange or turns slightly purple: the rates nearly balance.
Any change in tube D is far smaller than tube B's.

low.restatement: Purple means the leaf drained carbon dioxide; yellow means it filled the tube with it.
low.analogy: A bath with the plug half out: the water level's direction tells you which flow is winning.
low.examPointer: Attach a rate conclusion to every colour — photosynthesis greater, respiration greater, or balanced.

medium.restatement: Colour, then direction, then the rate verdict — the three-step reading.
medium.analogy: A thermometer reading that you then translate into hotter or colder weather.
medium.examPointer: Practise writing B, C and D conclusions in full sentences with the rate comparison.

check.stem: Why does tube B's indicator turn purple?

options.text: Photosynthesis outpaces respiration, so carbon dioxide drops below atmospheric
options.explanation: The leaf drains the sealed air's carbon dioxide.

options.text: The leaf releases extra carbon dioxide in light
options.explanation: Light shifts the balance towards carbon dioxide consumption.

options.text: The indicator decomposes in bright light
options.explanation: Light does not decompose the indicator.

options.text: The leaf absorbs the indicator itself
options.explanation: The leaf exchanges gases, not the solution.

check.stem: What does tube C's yellow colour prove?

options.text: Respiration alone ran, adding carbon dioxide above atmospheric
options.explanation: Darkness left respiration unopposed.
Foil blocks the light that photosynthesis needs.
The control rules contamination out.
Respiring leaves are alive; yellow is their normal night story.

check.stem: Which tube would end closest to its starting colour?

options.explanation: The control never changes, and the balanced leaf barely does.
Tube B swings all the way to purple.
Tube C swings all the way to yellow.
Two of the four change dramatically.

check.stem: What does a slightly purple tube D indicate?

options.text: Photosynthesis is just ahead of respiration in the dim light
options.explanation: A small net intake tints the indicator faintly purple.

options.text: Respiration is much larger than photosynthesis
options.explanation: That would push the colour towards yellow.
Cloth passes gases freely in both directions.
Drying is not part of the reading.

check.stem: Why are the tubes left overnight rather than read immediately?

options.text: The exchange is slow, and hours of accumulation make the colour change visible
options.explanation: Small net flows need time to move the indicator.

options.text: Because leaves only respire at night
options.explanation: Leaves respire at all hours.

options.text: Because the indicator is light-sensitive before then
options.explanation: The indicator's change tracks carbon dioxide, not waiting time.

options.text: To let the leaves dry out
options.explanation: Drying would damage the leaf, not help.

check.stem: State the expected final colour of each tube.
check.modelAnswer: A orange, B purple, C yellow, D orange or slightly purple.

check.stem: Give the rate conclusion behind tube B's colour.
check.modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is greater than respiration, so there is a net intake of carbon dioxide and its level falls.

check.stem: Explain why tube D changes less dramatically than tube B.
check.modelAnswer: Because dim light brings photosynthesis close to respiration, so the net carbon dioxide movement is small; tube B's bright light leaves photosynthesis far ahead, moving the level much further in the same hours.

check.stem: A muslin is replaced by thicker cloth that lets almost no light through. Predict tube D's new colour and justify.
check.modelAnswer: The tube would turn yellow like tube C: with almost no light, photosynthesis nearly stops and respiration alone keeps releasing carbon dioxide, so the sealed air's level climbs above atmospheric.

lessons.title: The Results Table and CORMS
sourceHeadings: The Effect of Light on Net Gas Exchange in Plants Table
Applying CORMS evaluation to practical work
lessons.opening: A tidy write-up pairs every tube with its conditions, colours and conclusion — and the CORMS prompt checks the design itself: the Change is the light availability, the Organism is matched leaves, the Repeat guards reliability, the Measurements are the indicator's colour and the waiting time, and the Same list pins the indicator volume, leaf count and temperature.
keyPoints: The table maps each tube to conditions, initial colour, final colour and conclusion.
CORMS: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measurement, Same — the design checklist.
The change here is the light treatment each tube receives.
Leaves should match in species, age and size across the tubes.
Repeats and fixed volumes make the comparison trustworthy.

low.restatement: The table records the results; CORMS audits the design that produced them.
low.analogy: A scoreboard plus a referee's checklist — one records, the other verifies fairness.
low.examPointer: Run CORMS aloud for any practical question; each letter is a mark opportunity.

medium.restatement: CORMS turns a good guess into a defensible design.
medium.analogy: Preflight checks before take-off: run the letters, then fly the experiment.
medium.examPointer: Write the Same list with three concrete items — volume, leaf count, temperature.

check.stem: In CORMS, what is the Change for this experiment?

options.text: The availability of light for each tube
options.explanation: Light is the deliberately varied condition.
Volume belongs to the Same list.
Species is matched, not varied.
The waiting time is fixed, not varied.

check.stem: Why should the leaves match in species and size?

options.text: So differences in exchange rate come from the light treatment, not the leaf
options.explanation: Matched leaves keep the tubes comparable.
Appearance plays no role.

options.text: Because the tubes only fit one size
options.explanation: Tube capacity is not the reason.

options.text: Because indicator changes colour with leaf size
options.explanation: The indicator reads carbon dioxide, not size.

check.stem: What are the two Measurements in this design?

options.text: The indicator's colour change and the time allowed
options.explanation: One measures the result, the other the duration.
Those belong to matching, not measuring.
Those belong to the Same list.
Light is the Change; tube count is neither.

check.stem: Which items does the Same list of the design pin down?

options.text: Indicator volume, number of leaves and temperature
options.explanation: Those three are named controls for this experiment.
Light is the Change; foil thickness defines the treatment.
Those are the Measurements.
Leaf matching is an Organism concern.

check.stem: Why does the Repeat letter matter here?

options.text: Repeating the setup shows the colour pattern is reliable, not a one-off
options.explanation: A single run could be a fluke.
Fresh leaves are used; that is not the purpose.
Indicator shelf-life is not the concern.
Bungs seal the tubes; repeats are about confidence.

check.stem: Write out the CORMS letters with their meanings.
State three Same-list items for this experiment.
check.modelAnswer: The indicator volume per tube, how many leaves each tube gets, and the environmental temperature throughout.

check.stem: Explain why an uncontrolled temperature would damage this experiment's conclusions.
check.modelAnswer: Because temperature alters respiration rate directly, so a warmer tube's leaf would respire faster and push its indicator towards yellow for reasons that have nothing to do with the light treatment — the confounder would masquerade as the effect being tested.

check.stem: Draft the table's row for tube C, filling conditions, initial colour, final colour and conclusion.
check.modelAnswer: Conditions: leaf wrapped in aluminium foil, dark; initial colour orange; final colour yellow; conclusion: no photosynthesis without light, respiration alone releases carbon dioxide, its level rises above atmospheric.

glossary.definition: A colour gauge for carbon dioxide: yellow at high, orange at atmospheric, purple at low levels.
The leaf-free tube establishing the indicator's unaltered colour.
The practical design checklist: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measurement, Same.
